lead: Abrasive water jet machining (AWJM) cuts metal, glass, stone and composites with a jet of water moving faster than sound, carrying abrasive grains. Only the jet touches the work, so cutting force is very small, there is no heat affected zone, and light clamping is enough. A high-pressure pump and intensifier push water at a few hundred MPa through a tiny orifice; abrasive is drawn in below the orifice and accelerated down a mixing tube. The jet erodes a narrow slot as the nozzle traverses.
prereq: Bernoulli's equation and continuity from fluid mechanics; surface finish comparison in Unit 5, grinding and finishing.

blocks.text: Water alone at high pressure cuts foam, rubber, cardboard and food: plain water jet cutting. Hard materials need abrasive. Garnet grains join the jet and strike at several hundred metres per second. Each grain chips a tiny fragment and the water carries debris out. Removal is erosion, not melting or shearing.

Near the top the jet is fast and coherent, cutting a slot about its own width. Deeper down it slows and loses coherence; only the core erodes, so the cut narrows. The top of the kerf (slot) is wider than the bottom, and jet lag shows as curved striations. Thick parts need slower traverse so the jet reaches the bottom.

The cut face is matt, a few micrometres roughness when cutting is slow. There is no recast layer, no dross burr like laser cutting, and no heat microcracks. Thin sheet may show a small exit burr, easily removed.

sections.h3: Building the pressure and the jet

blocks.text: A motor-driven pump takes water to about 20 MPa. A hydraulic intensifier multiplies this: a large-area hydraulic piston pushes a small-area plunger on the same rod, so output pressure is input pressure times the area ratio. A ratio of 15 gives 300 MPa from 20 MPa. Two intensifier cylinders alternate so one pumps while the other refills; a gas-charged accumulator absorbs pulses and steadies the jet.

Working pressure is 150 to 400 MPa, that is 1500 to 4000 bar. Compressed water at these pressures stores much energy; a pinhole leak can inject water through skin. Never put a hand near a pressurised line.

blocks.where: v is jet velocity at the orifice exit in m/s; P is water pressure in Pa; ρ is water density in kg/m³, about 1000 kg/m³. This is Bernoulli's equation with upstream velocity taken as zero.

blocks.text: The orifice is a sapphire or diamond disc with a hole 0.1 to 0.4 mm across; it wears and is replaced. Below it the jet enters the mixing (focusing) tube: tungsten carbide or composite, 50 to 100 mm long, 0.5 to 1.5 mm bore. Abrasive from a hopper passes a metering valve into the mixing chamber, and the fast jet drags grains in by a venturi effect and accelerates them down the tube. Abrasive never enters the pump or orifice; it would destroy the high-pressure seals.

Standoff distance is the gap between mixing tube exit and work, usually 1 to 5 mm. Small standoff keeps the jet coherent, giving narrow kerf and good accuracy; too small and the nozzle can strike the work. Traverse rate (mm/min) sets dwell time, hence depth of cut and taper.

Garnet is the usual abrasive: hard, cheap, breaks into sharp fragments. Grain size uses FEPA or mesh scale, typically 80 mesh for fine finish and 60 or coarser for speed. Abrasive flow is about 0.2 to 0.6 kg/min: too little wastes jet energy, too much chokes the mixing tube.

sections.h3: Why it is used, and where it stops

items: No heat affected zone or thermal distortion: good for thin sheet, titanium and composites that burn under a laser.
Very small cutting force, so thin flexible parts need only light clamping.
Narrow kerf, often 0.8 to 1.5 mm: little material loss, easy nesting.
Cuts almost any material: metals, glass, ceramics, stone, composites, stacked layers.
Can pierce mid-sheet and follow any CNC contour.

blocks.text: Capital and running costs are high: the pump draws tens of kilowatts, orifice and mixing tube wear out in tens to hundreds of hours, and abrasive is consumed continuously. The process is essentially a through cut; blind pockets are slow. Accuracy about ±0.1 to ±0.2 mm and taper are poorer than milling. Noise can exceed 85 dB and the spray carries fine abrasive mist.

Against laser cutting: a laser is faster and more precise on thin sheet but leaves a heat affected zone and possible recast layer. AWJ is slower but cuts thick sections, reflective metals such as aluminium and copper, and composites without heat damage. A laser cannot cut thick stone; water jet can. Choose by material, thickness and whether heat damage matters, not by speed alone.

Applications include marble and stone slabs with decorative profiles, glass cut without chipping, aerospace composites and titanium, gaskets, and food or plastics cut by plain water jets. Some shops turn and mill with a small abrasive jet under CNC control, the nozzle held in a tool holder.

examples.question: Water at 300 MPa enters the orifice of an abrasive water jet machine at 4 L/min. Take water density as 1000 kg/m³. (a) Find jet velocity at the orifice exit. (b) Find hydraulic power delivered by the pump. (c) The intensifier is fed hydraulic oil at 20 MPa. What area ratio does it need?
steps: Area ratio = 300 ÷ 20 = 15, so plunger area is one-fifteenth of piston area.
Check: 774.6 m/s is about 2.3 times the speed of sound in air, the right order for an AWJ jet at 300 MPa.
examples.answer: Jet velocity = 774.6 m/s, hydraulic power = 20 kW, intensifier area ratio = 15.
examples.check:
import math
P = 300e6
Q = 4.0 / 1000.0 / 60.0
v = math.sqrt(2 * P / 1000.0)
print(round(v, 1), round(P * Q / 1000.0, 1), 15.0)

examples.question: A 60 mesh garnet abrasive is fed at 0.30 kg/min into the mixing tube of the previous machine. Traverse rate is 120 mm/min and kerf width is 1.2 mm. (a) How much abrasive is used per metre of cut? (b) What area of new surface is created per second, counting one cut face only?
steps: Traverse rate = 120 mm/min = 2.0 mm/s, so one metre takes 1000 ÷ 120 = 8.333 min.
Abrasive per metre = 0.30 kg/min × 8.333 min = 2.5 kg.
New face per second = kerf width × traverse rate = 1.2 mm × 2.0 mm/s = 2.4 mm²/s, about 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s.
That 2.5 kg garnet per metre is why abrasive consumption dominates running cost.
examples.answer: Abrasive use is 2.5 kg per metre of cut, and the cut face is created at 2.4 mm²/s.

traps: Putting abrasive through the pump or orifice. It is entrained in the mixing tube, after the orifice, so it never touches high-pressure seals.
Unit slip on pressure: 300 MPa is 3000 bar, and 1 MPa = 10⁶ Pa, not 10⁵.
Confusing jet velocity with traverse rate: the jet moves at hundreds of m/s, the nozzle at a few mm/s.
Thinking a small standoff hurts accuracy. A standoff of 1-3 mm gives narrower kerf and less taper.
Claiming AWJ leaves a heat affected zone or recast layer. It erodes, so the work stays near room temperature; that is its main selling point over laser cutting.

quiz.q: Name the components that raise the water pressure, and the one that steadies it, in an abrasive water jet machine.
quiz.a: The high-pressure pump raises water to an intermediate pressure and the intensifier multiplies it to cutting pressure. The gas-charged accumulator absorbs pulses and steadies the flow.

quiz.q: Why is abrasive added after the orifice rather than before it?
quiz.a: Hard grains would abrade pump seals, valves and the small orifice and wear them out quickly. Adding abrasive in the mixing tube lets the clean high-speed jet draw grains in and accelerate them, so only the cheap replaceable tube sees the abrasive.

quiz.q: Explain why an AWJ cut is slightly tapered, with the top wider than the bottom.
quiz.a: Near the top the jet is fast and coherent, so it cuts a slot about the width of the jet. Deeper down it slows and loses coherence, only its core still erodes, and the cut narrows. So the top of the kerf is wider than the bottom, and jet lag shows as curved striations.

quiz.q: Water at 250 MPa and density 1000 kg/m³ leaves an orifice. Find the jet velocity.
quiz.a: v = √(2P ÷ ρ) = √(2 × 250 × 10⁶ ÷ 1000) = √(500 000) = 707.1 m/s, about twice the speed of sound in air.

quiz.q: An intensifier receives oil at 18 MPa and must deliver water at 360 MPa. What area ratio is needed, and if the water plunger area is 30 mm², what is the piston area?
quiz.a: Area ratio = 360 ÷ 18 = 20. Piston area = 20 × 30 mm² = 600 mm².

quiz.q: A shop must cut 25 mm thick carbon-fibre composite panels for an aircraft fairing. Compare abrasive water jet and laser cutting for this job and justify a choice.
quiz.a: Laser cutting is fast and precise on thin sheet, but heat chars the resin, leaves a heat affected zone and can delaminate the composite, so the edge needs trimming. AWJ erodes at near room temperature: no charring, no heat delamination, no heat affected zone, and the small force does not distort the panel. AWJ is slower and consumes garnet, but for a 25 mm structural composite it gives an acceptable edge in one pass. Choose AWJ, with slower traverse and higher abrasive flow to control taper.

quiz.q: Increasing traverse rate raises productivity but reduces depth of cut and worsens finish, widening taper. Explain this trade-off and state what you would change to cut a thicker part at the same quality.
quiz.a: A slow traverse lets the jet dwell, so it fully penetrates, the bottom of the cut catches up with the top, and the face is smoother with less taper. A fast traverse leaves the jet lagging: shallower cut, deeper striations, more taper. For a thicker part at the same quality, raise pressure, raise abrasive flow up to saturation, and reduce standoff, rather than only slowing the traverse, which costs productivity.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research models AWJ erosion with computational fluid dynamics coupled to particle tracking, so taper can be predicted and compensated in the CNC path. Five-axis machines tilt the nozzle to cancel taper, and some add a second angled jet. Micro-AWJ uses orifices below 0.1 mm for thin wafers and medical implants. Hybrid variants add a laser or cryogenic jet to soften the work ahead of the water. Search for 'AWJ taper compensation', 'abrasive water jet turning' and 'CFD erosion modelling'.
